name: Royal Palaces of Abomey
subtitle: A cultural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1985.

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “From 1625 to 1900, 12 kings succeeded one another at the head of the powerful Kingdom of Abomey. With the exception of King Akaba, who had his own separate enclosure, they all had their palaces built within the same cob-wall area, in keeping with previous palaces as regards the use of space and materials. The royal palaces of Abomey are a unique reminder of this vanished kingdom.”

A 2023 popular-history article says two traditions recorded in the 18th century give different founders for Abomey: the chief Dakodonu, who died in 1645, or Houegbadja, the first king of Dahomey, who reigned from 1645 to 1685.

It lists the succession as Houegbadja, Akaba (1685–1708), Agaja, Tegbesu (1740–1774), Kpengla (1774–1789), Agonglo (1789–1797), Adandozan, Gezo (1818–1858), Glele (1858–1889) and Béhanzin (1889–1894).
The complex held about a dozen royal residences and many other buildings. The article puts it at over a hundred acres, inside a city wall about 30 feet tall that ran for some 2.5 miles.

When the French army marched on Abomey in 1892–94, the same article says, Béhanzin saw that resistance was futile, left to set up a capital in the north, and ordered the palace complex razed, preferring that to leaving the sacred tombs and soul-houses to the enemy.

gaps: A specialist history of Dahomey to confirm the dates of the reigns, which differ between published lists, and the account of the 1892–94 war.
The museum today: what it shows, who runs it and how it tells this history.
The 2007 removal from the Danger List, and the restoration work since (the sources found are summaries, not the reports).
